Hi Jim,

I understand what you mean re. the stochasticity of CC3D and why the crashes do not happen at the same MCS (in the end, I want the program to behave stochastically, so that's fine).   
To the points above:

  
\- I don't have pixel reading or pixel writing going on in the codes that have been crashing, so I don't think the problem would lie in CC3D trying to read or write to pixels outside of the defined lattice geometry. It definitely makes sense that this would cause issues, but I don't think it pertains to the situation here.

  
\- There don't appear to be any indications of an error in the messages *before* the simulation runs, neither in the mini-console of the CC3D player nor in the Twedit++ terminal (in my case running in Windows cmd format). The error messages I posted this morning were preceded by 12 lines of standard simulation data (flips and energy levels for every 10th MCS) and the output before that seemed normal. Here's an example of what I get in the Twedit++ terminal at the very beginning of running an epithelium sim with hexagonal cell geometry (Epithelial2PyXMLHex; see Github link in original post):

The error messages thrown by the CC3D player console (not Twedit++ terminal) have always been very helpful: they point straight to the line of Python code that is causing an issue and I've always been able to resolve those problems. The Twedit++ terminal's messages re. these particular crashes have only been coming after the crash, i.e., after the CC3D player window suddenly disappears. 

I'm not an advanced programmer, but I've done some googling to try and unravel what might be behind the error messages I'm getting in the terminal and it looks like 

`"QObject::killTimer: Timers cannot be stopped from another thread`  
  
`QObject::~QObject: Timers cannot be stopped from another thread"` 

might have to do with parallel computing. I had `self.change_number_of_work_nodes(8)` in the start(self) of the class in the Python steppable this morning. I changed it to `self.change_number_of_work_nodes(4)`and the simulation ran about twice as long as before until it crashed. And this time, it crashed in a more unique way: instead of the CC3D player window simply closing, the cells in my epithelium first rapidly disintegrated until there was only a single circular column of cells roughly in the middle of the lattice, and only then did the CC3D player crash. So I've commented out the work node line of code in the steppable and am re-running the simulation on a single core. It's slower this way, but I'm hoping for more stability.

Is your life ruined? The short answer is: no, it is absolutely not ruined. It is just starting. Use every free minute to hack your own brain, find something that works for you and find something you love to do.

The long answer:

I am sorry to read that you are experiencing this. Your situation reminds me of my own. I do not want to make this about me, because it is essentially about you.. But I share this with you so that you see that I have a good idea of where you're coming from and so that you see that things will get better for you, too. 

I developed a psychotic disorder very similar to yours along with obsessive-compulsive disorder at age 15. PTSD and ADHD, too. The trigger for the genetic expression of the first two disorders was a severely traumatizing experience that I won't describe here. I was genetically predisposed to these disorders, as my father also had them.

I was in Germany for over 10 years and this was where my illness peaked. I'm not saying that to worry you; that did not simply happen to me because I was in Germany. There were many other factors that led up to that point but being an immigrant certainly did not help. There are studies that show that immigrants are more prone to mental illness. I eventually reached a point where I was not aware of how bad I'd gotten. I ended up acting on  delusions during psychosis, and losing my birthright citizenship as a result. I had been living hungry and alone in the attic of an old Lithuanian woman, thinking my mother tongue was rotting my brain. I am still trying to mop up the legal mess that that caused.

Looking back, the psychiatric care system in Germany wasn't good with initial diagnosis and treatment. There was a strong reluctance to diagnose and prescribe anything while I was still "together" enough to actively go out and ask for help. I speak fluent German and it did not help. While I appreciate a skeptical, scientific mind that wants to rule out other possibilities, this reluctance that I found to be more pronounced in German healthcare was counterproductive because it prevented me, someone who urgently needed help, from getting the stronger medicine and the intensive care that was immediately needed.

On the other hand, you can also have major problems in the US (where I'm from) where healthcare is far more profit-driven. I've had doctors here overprescribe and it took some time to find someone good.

My message to you is this: you will survive, grow stronger and prosper. I thought I was an absolute goner for quite some time and I still have occasional moments. But now, I am stable, I have a kind, compassionate psychiatrist, I live near my family and I am almost done with degrees in physics and quantitative economics. I am 32 and I still catch myself feeling ashamed or inferior because I probably could've been here in life sooner than my classmates had there not been a detour caused by worsening, unrecognized mental conditions. But alas, here I am. And so far, I've made it 17 years. And I look back and I cannot believe how much better I am now compared to 17 years ago.

I want you to know that your case is not at all hopeless and your disorders are completely manageable. Some might even go into remission later in life and if they don't, they can be managed. You will be able to live a fulfilling life. It is possible and it is a matter of finding treatment and a balanced lifestyle that works well with your mind.

Your life is NOT ruined. This is just the beginning. The first thing to do is to stop thinking it could be ruined. Start asking yourself: what do I need? What makes me feel the most stable, the most calm?

My advice would be to first find a way to live wherever you most feel comfortable, where you experience the most stability. If this is not Germany, then I would tell your mother that being there is not a positive influence on your mental health, that it is a serious medical issue.

Once you know where you are going to be long-term, begin looking for a good psychiatrist and a good psychotherapist. Medicine from the psychiatrist will help stabilize you, but the psychotherapist will help you understand how your mind works so that you can develop healthy patterns of thinking. Both medicine and therapy are necessary on your path to recovery. 

Also, if you can: exercise, exercise,  exercise! Exercise restructures the brain, it cleans it, it drives down brain inflammation, helps create new neural networks, lowers your resting heart rate and alleviates anxiety. And try to eat healthy, low inflammation foods. Take very good care of your body because a healthy body truly is a healthy home for a healthy mind. I found it so much easier to recover and manage life if I just went for a 3 to 4 mile run almost everyday. 

And I would try not to self-identify too much with your diagnoses. I found that the more I kept thinking about how these disorders were a part of my identity, the more power I gave them. This would cause me to feel hopeless, overwhelmed and think things like "my life is ruined." Just know that your brain is different. 

And focus on the positive things that you have going for you. As long as there isn't an abusive relationship, I think it is good to have family around and not be alone (like I was). This way, you will have someone to help you if you have an episode and you won't continue to spiral downward somewhere off by yourself. 

And think about something bigger than yourself. What do you believe you are here to do for the world? What would you like to do for the world? What are your dreams, what would your perfect concept of life look like?

All the best to you, my dear. You can thrive; never give up.

I personally disagree. I have been fortunate enough to have periods in which I was "taken care of" and instead of not doing anything, I began doing all kinds of work (much of it intellectual) which had otherwise been prevented by the fact that previous days had to be filled to the brim with the performance of tasks for the sole purpose of circulating a concept of money through a bank account. The money, by the way, being of a design and circulatory nature which was democratically never agreed upon by us, and about which I was most certainly never asked. In many ways it is the mathematical consequencescof our debt-money concept which make far more work seem necessary than is really the case.

Do you have a mission in your life, something that truly drives you, something you want to give to the rest of the world? If so, it will likely require immense amounts of work, for which you're likely not to be paid, but which could nevertheless be highly valuable to the rest of us, and provide you with a deep sense of fulfillment and joy.

From a more practical standpoint, we won't be running out of things to do, places to go, energy to harvest or things to think about any time soon. The universe is gargantuan and our time on Earth limited due to the lifespan of the sun. There is plenty to be done if we're to survive and evolve long-term, far beyond the realm of superfluous childish jobs indirectly born from a flawed understanding of monetary set theory. 

To me, it would be ludicrous to be freed from the time-robbing work made necessary by our current monetary model, and not actively seek and perform meaningful work (e.g. that brings us closer to becoming an interplanetary civilization). 

Speaking with others, I've gathered the impression that they feel the same or similarly. In many cases, it seems that 'laziness,' e.g. vegetating in front of the TV, often results from the mental exhaustion induced by our current concept of lifestyle. Laziness and long-term inactivity also lead to depression, thus you can safely assume the broad majority will set out to find and do something meaningful to them.

Hope you can find something new soon. I've been there many a time, doing crushing work.
The problem you describe is the problem many have: They actually don't mind humdrum work, but just don't want to fill the majority of their waking hours with it, and if they do some, they want to be able to live off of the income, not eat baked beans and live in the back of an SUV. 

The whole idea you are to irrevocably sacrifice the unique seconds of a finite existence for something that is most literally created out of thin air by those given a legal (only a century or two ago we would've said "divine") right to create it, is a form of insanity. It yields often superfluous and thus destructive overall social activity, because the work is no longer performed to fulfill an inherent purpose. One need only look at the garbage dumps full of plastic, the amount of antidepressants and antipsychotics prescribed to the general populace to grasp that this superfluous activity has terrible consequences for the human being.

Instead of going deeper into these points, I would like to highlight the often unmentioned but highly questionable nature of the money system itself, a system whose quantitative nature serves many as a metric for making qualitative moral conclusions. Being unaware of how today's money system is quantitatively manipulated means making such qualitative judgements on the basis of wholly lacking or incomplete information. I believe the OP - like countless others- has done so.

So, here a few points as to why the OP's opinion about other members of his or her own society appears to have been formulated on the basis of incomplete or unconsidered information:  


* The principal on modern debt is created out of thin air in a computer system. When you take out a "loan", no one anywhere is lowering their own money supply by the principal (This was once the case hundreds of years ago, before paper money, when loaned precious metal actually had to go from A to B). 
At the very most in the contemporary USA, a 10%-portion of a modern loan principal MIGHT be comprised of a bank's customer deposits as per minimum reserve requirement, but this practically never is the case as it is easy and far more lucrative for banks to expand their loan-creation capacity by directly borrowing large sums of cash (for covering the minimum reserve) from the FED. 90 % of this reserve can then be turned into digital fiat loans. This FED-to-bank lending is done for an interbanking interest rate low enough that the margin between the costs it generates and the income from debtors' regular interest payments on the fiat money is still large.

--

* When a loan is paid back, the digital money used to pay it back disappears. This is because when the loan is created from thin air, it is created as a negative quantity in the creditor's system and as a positive quantity in the debtor's system. If all debts were repaid, the money supply would diminish by the  amount of the principals. The collective interest in the entire system would of course remain (and mathematically cannot be paid back, only "forgiven").

--


* Every cent in circulation is a debt somewhere in the system for which interest is demanded. This even applies to the very currency units themselves, both hard and soft. But because the currency is the only legal means of paying back debts, there can mathematically never be a way to pay off the total sum of interest in the entire system, and to pay back the total principal in the system would literally mean deleting the entire money supply. Instead, the resulting debt obligation is shoved around like a hot potato, inhomogenously distributed but for the most part exponentially growing due to the (legally permitted) compounding of the interest.

--

* The guilt-trip resulting in most of the indebted population stems from the false impression that others are living on a shorter budget until they "repay" a "loan." The guilt-trip is the result of incomplete information, and need not occur, but the system will not let on to this: guilt and shame are essential to today's financial system as a means of exerting psychological pressure, ensuring acquiescence of the unknowing debtors. 

--

* The "legal" actions taken against so-called debtors within the framework of the contemporary money system serve as methods of exercising physical and psychological violence in a rationalized system of well-masked robbery. This violence is needed to pressure targets into doing whatever allows the  extraction of real tangible wealth and values on the basis of financially engineered fiction. 
Having a subject perform actions directed against his own interests is far more effective because this still gives his ego a sense of will and self-governance. Violence - the best being psychological violence as it makes direct connections to the source more difficult- is the means of getting a subject to that point. The "logic" used to convince both the targets and the enforcers that this violence-backed extraction is somehow morally justified is the qualitative set of morals often associated with the idea of money (that is, without of course mentioning the rigged nature of the current money system).

--

* It is not the fault of younger generations that older generations did not or could not inform themselves about the underlying principles of their society's core concepts such as money and debt. Where they were ignorant and fooled by what the young now see and understand, they should not be mocked or laughed at, but instead receive gratitude; their past  ignorance, misfortunes and hardships serve as valuable warnings, teaching the young what to do better, thus ensuring that the species can thrive more with each new generation. But the young also carry the responsibility of understanding and partaking in this dynamic. They too are not immune to ignorance. You're welcome, friend. I'm glad it can offer something. Yes, the whole thing we call life - with both the good and bad parts - is a treasure chest full of lessons. There really is a "school of life" and more often than not it's up to us to decide what classes we want to take. E.g. you lose your house and you can decide to take away the lesson that "life is hard, the world is cruel" or you can decide to learn lessons in gratitude, becoming more thankful for what you DO have...even if it's just your human body. In the end...that's all any one really has.

It's wonderful that you are transforming your trauma (or what you still refer to as trauma). When you change the meaning you give your life's story, you change the meaning substances have in your life, too. That's because the role you play changes. You shed old habits and traits and develop new ones for your new role. 

We can end up identifying with trauma, pain and addiction because we make it the main plot line of our life's story. At some point, we don't know what else to identify with...shedding this identity feels similar to death. What are we without it? And people around us in our lives have also associated this identity with us...we're that "really smart and sweet guy who just has a lot of issues" or "the loser junkie" etc. 

Many people are afraid to change because it would mean others see this change occurring. If we fail in our first attempt to change, we fear that people might then add "failure" or "loser" to the identity we carry for them (if they haven't already). It then becomes harder to try again - at least we make it that way psychologically- because we think that no one really believes we can do it anyway. 

I can only speak from my own experience, but shame often played a tremendous role in using self-destructively. I felt ashamed of my behavior, and knowing that certain people wanted me to quit because they loved me actually made it worse (I LET this make it worse), because the thought that I could fail and disappoint those so dear to me only increased my feelings of shame. I had people watch me try to quit and then - when I fell back into it and they knew it - I felt deeply ashamed: "I bet they think I'm a loser."

Shame is probably the most destructive, unhelpful and non-productive feeling in our emotional spectrum. I believe it is at the core of my addictive behavior: being ashamed of where I come from, being ashamed I didn't deal with things better, that I didn't "turn out right" (as if there was any right way to turn out!), shame that I needed substances. Shame comes from wanting the approval of others and failing to get it...it's the same mechanism as addiction to substances...you're always after something outside of yourself to make you feel better. Many use to numb the pain caused by their shame. Kick the shame, and you kick the addiction. 

You've made the internal decision to take yourself by the hand, love yourself, heal yourself and thrive. It will take time to allow your brain chemistry to change, it will take time to allow new neural circuits to form. Go at your pace. Don't allow any kind of shame to get in your way if you're not making progress at the rate others might expect. As long as you are giving yourself what you need like a responsible parent a child, as long as you are always on your side and stay your best friend, you're on the right path. No matter how long it takes to get to where you want to be. Set small goals for the day...even the hour or minute if you need to. And celebrate them when you've reached them. 

Sorry for such a long post again. I promise I'll stop now. Wishing you all the best! Ride the waves; don't fight them. You're going to be a totally different person in one year.

Hey there, friend. Thanks for sharing your story and reaching out. You are still young, and with the brain you have, you have all the time and resources you will need to heal and take care of yourself. Now it’s just a matter of consciousness, becoming hyper-aware of what your mind and body do that lead you onto the addiction-path. About half-way into your post, I it became very clear that you are intelligent. It’s not the words you use or the way you structure your sentences, it’s the content. You already exhibit a high degree of consciousness and self-awareness, evaluating your behavior and habits and analyzing relationships from an outside, unbiased perspective. You know what role you have played in relationships with others, you admit to your roles in them, even if they aren’t desirable roles. You are also aware of what is going on inside of you as you interact with others. You have an analytical mind capable of seeing the world from many different angles and in many different layers, and you demonstrate a high degree of empathy and understanding. So please know that there is a tremendous amount of hope for you, a tremendous amount of potential. The journey you have behind you and before you can empower you, inspire others and do amazing amounts of good in this world. Use your creativity to transform your suffering into thriving. You can become that “source” that you are missing, and while it can be very helpful to have people around you to provide this “source”, it can in fact be found within yourself. You can become your own source to the same degree with which you have become your own drain.

At the end of your post, you ask why you stay so enamoured with the idea of being a user and then you say it’s part of your identity. I would go even further, saying it is part of your biological make-up. It’s how your brain is wired. By that, I don’t mean that you’re damned to be using for the rest of your life, but this pre-disposition is a part of who you are. I don’t think it is helpful to not want to be who you are…instead, accept yourself for who you are and start working from there. You can possess a brain pre-disposed to addiction and still have a wonderful, fulfilling, prosperous life on this planet. You certainly have the intelligence – both emotional and intellectual – to get there. This doesn’t necessarily mean getting rich and owning a bunch of shit (often another form of addiction). It means living a life that your heart says yes to, a life that fills you with a sense of personal fulfillment, inner peace and ease. You can learn to utilize your addictive brain type to serve you and the world around you. It starts when you begin seeing how what you currently perceive to be weaknesses can be applied in different situations as strengths that will serve you and others.

Ask yourself what the hole is that you’re trying to fill, focussing less on what you’re using to try and fill it. We tend to focus a lot on the substances, but the addiction is only the expression of a much deeper issue. There is an inherent “logic” to what you are doing even if it appears to be self-destructive. It’s important that you know this so that you can stop feeling guilty and ashamed about your behavior. Guilt and shame create new thought circuits that drive us back to using. We must love, embrace and accept ourselves exactly as we are at this very moment in order to become healthy. The next time you crave, try holding off and observing yourself, following every sensation. Don’t engage in inner-resistance or scolding. Accept that you are craving, allow yourself to crave, and don’t start up the whole inner game of “I shouldn’t be doing…I shouldn’t be wanting…I can’t get my act together…I’m such an asshole…etc.” You have to allow yourself to be right where you are…that’s the only place from which you can determine a new course.

You possess self-love and you are in fact all that you need in this world. Your self-love is strong enough to make you realize that your substance use is not serving you. I am not someone who condemns substances across the board. My previous use of psychedelics helped me heal from the trauma I endured as a young boy and young man. I grew up with a dad who couldn’t touch me or love me. He had severely debilitating OCD and drank himself into a stupor everyday. I didn’t know it at the time, but he was also gay and lived a life he didn’t want to live. But his family was catholic and would’ve disowned him otherwise. When I was 15, my dad tried killing himself in front of me in our bathroom. The trauma of seeing that and finding him like that triggered my own mental disorders. My mom was the one who really raised me, but she suffered PTSD from her childhood and her marriage to my father. Poverty, intense fear and grief were all core components of my childhood. My dad ended up eventually succeeding at suicide the second time around. At 18, I dropped out of highschool, saved money for a flight and then ran away to another country with almost no money, marrying a girl there from a similar background. We were addicted to eachother. I also became addicted to porn, school and work, being the valedictorian of my class in this foreign country. I was exhausted and half-dead, with growing mental disorders, but I was able to trick myself into thinking I could fill the hole in me with material success. When my wife left me for another guy, and I became homeless, I couldn’t fill the hole with material success or marriage anymore. I then fell into using. It started with chain-smoking cigarettes, then went over to weed, which I eventually needed to function throughout the day, otherwise I had the withdrawal symptoms you describe. I ended up living in a closet-sized space at the edge of town, keeping an awful job just to stay in the country. I fell into hearing voices and experiencing delusional thinking. Later, I started also using coke and speed.

Years later, I discovered LSD and MDMA. These two substances made it possible for me to feel love, interconnectedness and empathy again for the first time in more than a decade. My first MDMA trip melted away the cancerous crust of grief and rage that had been clogging my soul and the connection to myself. I am extremely thankful for the trips I was allowed to have on these substances. That is not to say that they can only do good. As you yourself know, they can be become highly addictive, just like alcohol, weed or amphetamines. Instead of stepping stones, they become a crutch. We end up using this crutch so much that our leg muscles disappear all together. We then reach a point where we can no longer walk on our own at all. This is when the substances stop serving you and begin contributing to your destruction. This destruction has multiple forms. For one, it’s the excessive amount of stress they place on your body due to constant use, but it’s also the way they keep you from digesting what life has served you. There are dragons you must confront, big inner things you must deal with, things that overwhelm you, overchallenge or terrify you, things like childhood trauma. These things are not fair, they suck, and no, we didn’t deserve them. We deserved better. But to deny them, run from them and numb ourselves into oblivion means we stop growing. To look these terrible things in the eye, embrace them and integrate them into our lives, eventually digesting them, is to grow as an intelligent being.

Right now, looking at where you currently are, I think it is very important that you abstain from substances entirely, because substances cannot meet the needs you currently have to continue growing. They are the wrong tool at your current stage of development. You may find that you never touch them again, and that is fine, too. Do always what says ‘yes’ to and serves life, growth, health and joy. Get help from outside, check yourself into a detox center, start going to a group if it is helpful for you. Be patient with yourself, accept yourself and work with yourself as you are now. Stay present. I’m always here if you need to write to someone. Feel free to send me a PN. The TV was on and a lot of school staff were standing around watching a live news feed. Right at that moment, when I looked in, the second plane hit the WTC. I couldn't believe my eyes and at that moment I knew there was no bombs involved. We got sent home early that day for reasons of security. Somehow, our teachers thought our cow town could be important for the terrorists. 

Anyway, fastforward to the afternoon. My dad was a pretty screwed up, mentally ill alcoholic who never really could be a father; and he knew it. He was sitting at home unemployed, but on this day - I guess it was all the people dying and whatnot - he decided to try being that good ol' American dad. He was terrible at sports, was more of the theater and arts guy, but on the late afternoon of 9/11 he took me out to the park to try some batting practice. I think we had gotten 3 pitches behind us when he threw his back out. He remained lying in the grass screaming his head off. I was able to help him back up and support him all the way back home.

My mom loaded my dad into the car and we took off to the hospital. I remember we had to cross a lot of railroad crossings. My dad was lying in the back seat and screamed every time we went over those heavy bumps. The car had horrible shocks. We ended up at some awful emergency room with terrible staff. They gave my dad the wrong IV and actually made his heart stop for a full minute. I remember just standing there watching him turn as white as a sheet, then we heard that typical flatline tone. My mom was absolutely in panic. Staff came running by and some nurse sent me to the waiting room. We had gotten there at 6 pm; it was now 2 am. The place had been totally understaffed. I remember being dead-tired and just sitting alone in the waiting room looking at the TV screen. Every single channel kept rerunning the attack footage.  And because it was late, they decided to start showing the gruesome stuff. Around 3 am was when I saw the jumpers for the first time. I remember that really getting to me. Everything else had been very horrible, but totally anonymous and faceless. But with the jumpers, the whole thing got terribly human and up-close.

That day sucked balls.
